newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan forex market grapples with EMU uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Japan forex market grapples with EMU uncertainty.

text.p: Japan is still struggling with too many unknowns about European monetary union to predict the impact of a single European currency on the yen and the home currency market, dealers and analysts say.
Although some fear the yen could be hurt by the new currency, the Euro, most say it is simply too early to tell.

"There's still so many issues left open -- what kind of countries will take part, what the government controls will be, how they will manage fiscal policy -- that it's extremely difficult to say what will happen," said Kenneth Landon, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Tokyo.

Toyoo Gyohten, a former vice minister of international affairs at Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF), said that while there was unlikely to be much immediate impact, over the long term the Euro could become quite significant.

"From Japan's point of view, we have to acknowledge the possibility that the Euro may become a formidable competitor. If the yen is not in a position to compete with the Euro, the yen may decline," he told a seminar in Tokyo last week.

Key for the market here in predicting the yen's competitiveness is which countries eventually qualify to take part in European economic and monetary union (EMU), which is set to start on January 1, 1999, as this will determine the strength of the Euro itself.

Current expectations are that EMU will initially include Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands -- which would result in a "hard" rather than "soft" Euro, analysts said.
A senior MOF official said that while the introduction of a hard Euro is most desirable from a world market view, it could negatively affect the yen.

"If it's a strong Euro, say somewhat like the mark's been up to now, there's the chance that many world central banks will think that it's better to hold Euros than yen in their foreign reserves," he said.
"If it's a soft Euro, this would lead to increased holdings of dollars or yen, and the yen could strengthen," he added.

A dealer with a European bank, who asked not to be identified, expressed the opinions of many in the market when he said that the impact on the yen is likely to depend mainly on what happens to the dollar, and that if the dollar rises, the yen may suffer.

But he added that he feels it is still premature to worry much about the issue. "Basically, I think it is impossible that they will be able to meet the criteria as planned and carry EMU off on schedule. And I believe it's hard for a majority of Tokyo traders to imagine it succeeding as well," he said.
Many in Tokyo confessed to uncertainties about EMU even if the single currency does go ahead as planned.

"Will this produce growth for Europe or the opposite, and what will happen to interest rates? Nobody can figure this out, and this will have a big impact on the currency," said Tomomitsu Oba, a former MOF vice minister of international affairs.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Landon agreed. "What determines the value (of a currency) is not just liquidity and efficiency but also the fiscal policy. The Euro will be under pressure from so many different interest groups and there's quite a large doubt in my mind about central bankers managing to work in a political vacuum."
But the Tokyo market's biggest single difficulty in grappling with EMU may be something as simple as indifference.

"Japanese banks should be a lot more concerned about this -- they're taking their own sweet time in getting around to thinking about it. They feel basically that this is a European question," Oba said.
